title: Secrets, Auth, and Security
summary: Keep secrets on the server, load environment variables correctly, protect pages and actions with sessions, and set security headers.
intro: A Next.js app holds things the browser must never see: API keys that cost money, the address of your API, the session that says who's logged in. Server Components and actions run on your server, which makes those secrets easier to keep than in a single-page app, and also easier to leak, since a server value is one prop away from the browser. This lesson covers where settings and secrets live and when they're read, how to call a paid API with a secret key, how to know who's calling with a session and a data access layer, where authorization checks belong, which security headers to send, and how to keep the framework itself patched.

steps.title: Environment variables and .env files
steps.body:
Your app needs settings that change from place to place. The API's address on your laptop is `http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1`, in production it's something else, and a secret key must never be written in your code or saved in git. The React course kept settings like these in **environment variables**, named values a program gets from its surroundings when it starts, and Vite gave the browser the ones whose names start with `VITE_`. Next.js works the same way, with two twists: your code runs on a server as well as in the browser, and some of it runs during the build.

## process.env and the .env files

On the server, every environment variable is in `process.env`, an object Node.js fills in when the program starts. `process.env.API_URL` is a string, or `undefined` when nothing set it. You can set variables in the terminal, like `API_URL=... npm run start`, or in your hosting platform's settings. On your own computer, Next.js also reads them from files in the project's root folder:

| File | Holds | Commit it? |
|---|---|---|
| `.env` | defaults for everyone | yes, with no secrets |
| `.env.local` | your own values and secrets | never |
| `.env.development`, `.env.production` | defaults for one mode | yes, with no secrets |
| `.env.development.local`, `.env.production.local` | your own values for one mode | never |
| `.env.test` | defaults for tests | yes |

The **mode** is the variable `NODE_ENV`. `next dev` sets it to `development`, `next build` and `next start` set it to `production`, and test runners set it to `test`.

When one name is set in several places, Next.js takes the first one it finds, in this order:

1. `process.env`, what was already set when the program started.
2. `.env.$(NODE_ENV).local`, like `.env.production.local`.
3. `.env.local`, which is skipped in the test mode, so tests run the same for everyone.
4. `.env.$(NODE_ENV)`, like `.env.production`.
5. `.env`.

So a variable set in the terminal beats every file, and your `.env.local` beats the shared `.env`. The build's second line names the files it loaded: `- Environments: .env.local, .env`. One gotcha: a `$` in a value refers to another variable, so `A=$B` copies `B`. Write `\$` for a real dollar sign, which matters for generated passwords.

## Committing the right files

The `.gitignore` that create-next-app writes ignores every file whose name starts with `.env`. To share safe defaults and a list of what the app needs, add exceptions under that line:

```text
.env*
!.env
!.env.example
```

`.env.example` lists every variable with an empty or fake value, as in the React course, so a new teammate knows what to fill in their own `.env.local`. Keep secrets out of both committed files.

## NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are baked into the bundle

Code in the browser has no `process.env`. As the lesson on Server and Client Components showed, a value reaches it only when the variable's name starts with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. During `next build`, Next.js finds each `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPPORT_EMAIL` in code that ships to the browser and replaces it with the value itself, written out as text, which is called **inlining**. The first example finds the value in the built JavaScript.

Two things follow. Every value with that prefix is public: anyone can read it in the files the browser downloads, exactly like the `VITE_` values. And it's frozen at build time: change it on the server afterward, and the browser keeps getting the old value until you build again. Only a written-out `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_NAME` is replaced, never a lookup like `process.env[name]`.

## Server values are read when code runs, and some runs at build

A variable without the prefix stays on the server, and your code reads it whenever it runs. But with Cache Components, a page that reads no request data is prerendered: it runs once, during `next build`, and every visitor gets that HTML. Whatever `process.env` held during the build is what the page shows, however you start the server later. The second example shows it happening.

To read a value per request, read it after `await connection()` from `next/server`, which says this part waits for a real request, inside a Suspense boundary like any request data. That matters when one build runs in several places, like a test server and production, each with its own values. The deployment lesson comes back to that.

examples.title: A public value, inlined into the bundle
examples.prompt: `components/support-link.tsx` is a Client Component that reads `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPPORT_EMAIL`, and `.env.local` holds a secret, `RATES_API_KEY`. After `npm run build`, search the browser's files for both. Mac and Linux.
examples.code:
grep -rho '.\{20\}help@trailhead.example.\{2\}' .next/static
grep -rl "rk_test_" .next/static || echo "not in the browser files"
examples.output:
0,function(){let e="help@trailhead.example";
not in the browser files
examples.explanation: `.next/static` holds the JavaScript, CSS, and fonts the browser downloads. In the first search, `-r` looks through every file in the folder, `-h` leaves out file names, `-o` prints only the match, and `.\{20\}` asks for the 20 characters before it. The built code says `let e="help@trailhead.example"`: the build shortened names, which is why the variable is called `e`, and the reference to `process.env` is gone, replaced by the value. The second search looks for the start of the secret key, finds nothing, and `||` runs the `echo`. A server variable never reaches the browser's files on its own. It only gets there when your code hands it over, which the next part shows.

examples.title: Read at build, or read per request
examples.prompt: `app/promo/page.tsx` shows `process.env.PROMO_TEXT`, and `app/promo/live/page.tsx` shows it after `await connection()`. `.env` sets it to Free shipping. Start the build with `PROMO_TEXT="Half price tents today" npm run start`, then fetch both pages from a second terminal.
examples.code:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3005/promo | grep -oE 'Free shipping[^<\\]*|Half price[^<\\]*' | sort -u
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3005/promo/live | grep -oE 'Free shipping[^<\\]*|Half price[^<\\]*' | sort -u
examples.output:
Free shipping on orders over 100 dollars
Half price tents today
examples.explanation: The first page was prerendered during the build, when `PROMO_TEXT` came from `.env`, so it still says Free shipping, even though the running server has the new value. Its line in the build's route table has ○, the static mark. The second page reads the variable after `await connection()`, so it reads `process.env` while answering and shows Half price tents today. In the command, `grep -oE` prints each match of either phrase, `[^<\\]*` stops at the next tag or escaped quote, and `sort -u` drops repeats, since the text also sits in the page's RSC payload. When a value has to change without a new build, read it per request.

steps.title: Secret keys stay on the server

examples.title: A Client Component imports a server-only module
examples.prompt: `components/rates-widget.tsx`, a Client Component, imports `env` from `@/lib/env` to show the rates API's address. Build, and keep the lines about the problem. Mac and Linux.
examples.code: npm run build 2>&1 | grep -A 18 "cannot be imported"
examples.output:
Error: 'server-only' cannot be imported from a Client Component module
> 1 | import "server-only";
    | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  2 | import { z } from "zod";
  3 |
  4 | const ServerEnv = z.object({

It should only be used from a Server Component.

Import traces:
  Server Component:
    ./lib/env.ts
    ./lib/rates.ts
    ./app/shipping/page.tsx

  Client Component Browser:
    ./lib/env.ts [Client Component Browser]
    ./components/rates-widget.tsx [Client Component Browser]
    ./components/rates-widget.tsx [Server Component]
examples.explanation: The build stopped at the guard's line in `lib/env.ts`. The import traces show the module's two lives. Under Server Component, the shipping page imports the rates client, which imports `lib/env.ts`, and that's fine. Under Client Component Browser, `rates-widget.tsx` imports it too, and that code would ship to the browser, secrets and all. The trace names the file to fix. Without the guard, the build would have bundled `lib/env.ts` for the browser, where `process.env.RATES_API_KEY` is `undefined`, and you'd have found out from a broken page instead of a clear error.

examples.title: A bad value stops the build
examples.prompt: Build with a key that doesn't start with rk_, set in the terminal for this one command, and print the output from where the build checks the pages. Mac and Linux.
examples.code: RATES_API_KEY=oops npm run build 2>&1 | sed -n '/Collecting page data/,$p'
examples.explanation: `RATES_API_KEY=oops` at the start sets the variable for this one command, and `process.env` beats `.env.local`, so the build sees the bad value. `sed -n '/Collecting page data/,$p'` prints from that line to the end, skipping the lines before it. The ZodError names the variable in `path` and says what's wrong in `message`, and the trace shows how the build got there: the account page imports the data access layer, which imports `lib/env.ts`. The value itself isn't printed, which is what you want from an error about a secret. A deploy with a missing key fails here, before any visitor sees a broken page.

examples.title: A key passed as a prop
examples.prompt: `app/leak/page.tsx` renders `<RatesButton apiKey={env.RATES_API_KEY} />`, a Client Component that logs the key when clicked. With the built app running, search the page for the key. Mac and Linux.
examples.explanation: The page passed the key to `RatesButton`, and there it is in the HTML, inside the RSC payload that React uses to hydrate the Client Component: `{"apiKey":"rk_test_4f9a2c7e1b8d"}`, with its quotes escaped because the payload sits inside a script. The page is static, so the key was also written into the prerendered files in `.next/server`, and any CDN that cached the page holds a copy. View source in a browser shows the same. The fix is never to send it: keep the call on the server and pass down only the rates.

steps.title: Sessions and a data access layer

examples.title: The data access layer
examples.prompt: `lib/dal.ts`: one cached session check, a strict version that redirects, and a DAL function that returns a small DTO.
examples.explanation: `cache(async () => ...)` wraps `getSession` so that, within one render, every caller shares the first call's answer. No cookie means no session, and so does a 401 from `/me`, which is what the API says for a made-up or expired ID. Any other failure is a real error, so it's thrown. The session object holds only an ID and a name, not the API's whole answer. `verifySession` is the strict version, and its return type promises a session, because `redirect` never returns. `getCartSummary` shows the DAL's pattern: check first, then fetch with the forwarded cookie and check the answer with zod, as `lib/products.ts` does, then shape a DTO with two fields. A page can't forget the check, because it's inside the function it calls.

examples.title: An account page that checks in each part
examples.prompt: `app/account/page.tsx`: a static shell, with the per-visitor parts inside a Suspense boundary.
examples.explanation: The heading, the fallback, and the logout form don't depend on the visitor, so they're prerendered into the page's static shell. `Greeting` and `Cart` read the session, so they render per request inside the boundary and stream in. Both ask for the session, and `cache()` makes that one `GET /me`. Each component checks for itself instead of trusting the page to have checked, so moving `Cart` to another page keeps it safe. The logout form posts to the `logout` action from `app/account/actions.ts` and works before JavaScript loads, like every form with a Server Action.

examples.title: The cookie, set and then cleared
examples.prompt: The login action's request and answer, then the logout action's, from a real browser, cut to the request line, the status, the redirect, and `Set-Cookie`.
examples.code:
POST /login HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-action-redirect: /account;push
Set-Cookie: th_session=860751a3-df04-4370-85ea-2dc124b676c2; Path=/; Expires=Sun, 29 Nov 2026 03:13:54 GMT; Max-Age=604800; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=lax

POST /account HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
x-action-redirect: /;push
Set-Cookie: th_session=; Path=/; Expires=Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:00:00 GMT
examples.explanation: These are the two Server Action calls that changed the cookie: logging in, then pressing Log out, captured from a real browser. Each is a POST to the page the form is on, answered 200 with an `x-action-redirect` for the router, as the Server Actions lesson showed. The first `Set-Cookie` sets `th_session` to the API's session ID, with a week's `Max-Age` and an `Expires` date to match, and all three flags. The second is what `cookies().delete()` sent: an empty value that expired in 1970, so the browser throws the cookie away. In DevTools, the Application panel's Cookies list shows the stored cookie with HttpOnly and Secure ticked, and no script on the page can read it with `document.cookie`.

steps.title: Authorization at every door
steps.body:
The previous part answered who is this. Many requests need a second answer too: may this visitor do this, which is **authorization**. And an app has more doors than its pages. Each page, each Server Action, and each Route Handler can be reached directly, by a browser or a script, and a check at one door protects only that door.

```diagram secrets-auth-security-checks
Proxy can turn visitors away early, but the data access layer decides.
```

## Check where the data is

Put the checks where the data is read, in the DAL, and call the DAL from every door:

- A page calls `verifySession()`, or a DAL function that does, before it renders anything private.
- A Server Action checks first thing, as the Server Actions lesson showed, since it's a way in of its own.
- A Route Handler can't send a script to a login page, so it calls `getSession()` and answers 401 when there's none, like the third example.

Authorization also means ownership. The Trailhead API answers `GET /v1/orders/{orderId}` with 404 when the order is someone else's, and your DAL should treat your own data the same way: look items up by their ID together with the session's user, never by the ID alone.

## Proxy checks only optimistically

The lesson on Route Handlers and proxy introduced `proxy.ts`, which runs before every request its matcher covers, and called its checks optimistic. Here's what that means in practice. Proxy is a good place to send visitors with no session cookie to the login page before anything renders, as the first example does. It checks that a cookie exists, not that it's valid, since asking the API on every request, prefetches included, would slow down the whole app.

So a made-up cookie gets through. The second example sends one: proxy let it in, the page started streaming, and then the page's own `verifySession()` sent the browser to the login page. That's why proxy is never the only check.

There's a second reason, and it happened. A **CVE**, short for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, is the public ID a security bug gets, so everyone can talk about the same one. In March 2025, Next.js published CVE-2025-29927: on self-hosted apps, a request with an internal header, `x-middleware-subrequest`, skipped middleware, proxy's old name, entirely. Apps that checked logins only in middleware had their private pages open to anyone who added that header. It was fixed in 15.2.3 and 14.2.25, with fixes for 13.5.9 and 12.3.5 too. Apps whose pages and actions checked the session themselves kept their data safe.

Matchers fail the same way, by accident. A Server Action is a POST to the page it's used on, so a matcher that leaves out a path also leaves out that page's actions, and moving a page can quietly move it out of proxy's reach.

## Layouts don't guard their pages

A check in a layout looks as if it covers every page inside it, and it doesn't. On a soft navigation between two pages that share a layout, Next.js renders only the new page and keeps the layout, as the routing lesson showed, so the layout's check doesn't run again. A layout also can't stop its pages from rendering: they render on their own, and their output goes into the RSC payload whatever the layout returns. Read the user in a layout to show their name, and check access in the pages and the DAL.

## unauthorized() and forbidden()

`notFound()` from the routing lesson throws to show the 404 page. Two experimental siblings do the same for 401 and 403: `unauthorized()` when there's no session, and `forbidden()` when the session isn't allowed. They need `experimental: { authInterrupts: true }` in `next.config.ts`, and they render `unauthorized.tsx` and `forbidden.tsx` files you write next to your pages. Being experimental, their details may still change. When the page has already started streaming, the status stays 200, and Next.js adds a `noindex` tag so search engines skip the page.

examples.title: An optimistic check in proxy
examples.prompt: `proxy.ts`, in the project's root folder, cut down to the login check from the lesson on Route Handlers and proxy: send visitors with no session cookie to the login page.
examples.explanation: The matcher limits proxy to `/account` and the paths under it. `request.cookies.has` only asks whether a `th_session` cookie came with the request, which takes no time and no network. With no cookie, proxy answers with a redirect to `/login`, with `next` set so the login action can send the visitor back afterward. Returning nothing lets the request carry on to the page. This saves a visitor who clearly isn't logged in a wasted render and a flash of the loading state. It decides nothing about a cookie that is there, which is the DAL's job.

examples.title: No cookie, and a made-up one
examples.prompt: With the built app running, ask for the account page with no cookie, then with a session ID nobody issued, then ask the cart's Route Handler with that same ID.
examples.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{redirect_url}\n" http://127.0.0.1:3005/account
curl -s -H "Cookie: th_session=made-up" http://127.0.0.1:3005/account | grep -oE '<meta id="__next-page-redirect"[^>]*>|Hi, [^<]*' | sort -u
curl -s -H "Cookie: th_session=made-up" http://127.0.0.1:3005/api/cart
examples.explanation: The first request has no cookie, and proxy answers 307 with the login page's address, so the page never renders. `-w` prints the status and where the redirect points. The second sends a session ID that the API never issued. Proxy saw a cookie and let it through, the page's shell was sent with a 200, and when `verifySession()` found no session, the redirect arrived inside the stream: a `meta` refresh tag pointing at `/login`, which also works without JavaScript, alongside a redirect for the router. The grep looked for the greeting too, and Hi never appears. The third asks the Route Handler, which checks with `getSession()` and answers with a 401 problem.

examples.title: A Route Handler that checks for itself
examples.prompt: `app/api/cart/route.ts`: the visitor's cart summary as JSON, or a 401.
examples.explanation: `app/api/cart/route.ts` is a door that scripts and other apps use, not just your pages, so it answers in HTTP's own terms. With no session, it returns a 401 with a small problem body, in the shape the Trailhead API uses for errors. With one, it returns the DTO from the DAL, which checks the session again inside `getCartSummary()`. That second check costs another `GET /me`, since `cache()` does nothing outside a render: one call to this handler showed two in the dev log. Proxy's matcher covers `/account` only, so this handler had no proxy check at all, and it didn't need one.

steps.title: Security headers and a CSP
steps.body:
Security headers tell the browser to refuse things your pages never need: scripts from other sites, being shown inside another site's frame, guessing what a file is. The React course met these headers and noted that the server sends them, not React. In Next.js, you run the server, so they're yours to send.

## Static headers in next.config.ts

`headers()` in `next.config.ts` returns lists of headers for path patterns, and Next.js adds them to every matching response, prerendered pages included. The first example sets them for every path. What each one does, as the React course explained:

- `Content-Security-Policy`, or **CSP**, lists where each kind of content may come from. `'self'` means your own origin. `frame-ancestors 'none'` stops other sites from framing your pages, the defense against clickjacking. `object-src 'none'` blocks plugins, and `form-action 'self'` keeps forms from posting anywhere else.
- `Strict-Transport-Security` is HSTS from the web course: HTTPS only, here for two years.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` makes the browser trust `Content-Type` instead of guessing.
- `Referrer-Policy` limits how much of your URL other sites see when a visitor follows a link away.
- `Permissions-Policy` switches off browser features the site never uses, like the camera.

`poweredByHeader: false` drops the `X-Powered-By: Next.js` header, one less hint for anyone probing your site. The second example shows the headers on a product page.

## Why script-src allows 'unsafe-inline'

The strictest policy would be `script-src 'self'`: scripts from your own files and nothing else. Next.js pages break under it. Next.js puts the RSC payload into the HTML as small **inline scripts**, `script` tags with code inside instead of a `src`, and `'self'` doesn't cover inline code. Tried on the product page, the browser console filled with "Executing inline script violates the following Content Security Policy directive 'script-src 'self''", once for each script, and the page never hydrated, so no button that needs JavaScript worked. Adding `'unsafe-inline'` allows inline scripts, which is what the example does. It also weakens the policy, since a script someone managed to inject would run too.

## Nonces: a strict policy, at a price

A **nonce** is a random value made fresh for each response. The policy says `script-src 'nonce-abc123'`, and the browser runs only the scripts whose `nonce` attribute matches. An injected script can't know this response's nonce, so it's blocked, while your own scripts run. Proxy makes the nonce and puts it in the policy on both the request and the response, and Next.js reads it from the request and adds it to every script it renders. The third example is that proxy.

The price is that every page has to be rendered per request, since a page built ahead of time can't hold a nonce made later. Tried with the product pages prerendered as usual, the HTML had no nonces, and the browser blocked every script. With Cache Components, the fix is to make the root layout wait for a request, with `await connection()` and `export const instant = false`. Then the build worked and the nonces appeared, and every route in the route table turned ƒ, dynamic, each answer marked `Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store`. That means no static shell, no CDN copies, and more work for your server on every visit. Choose nonces when the rules you work under demand a strict policy. Otherwise, the static headers above are the usual choice. Next.js also has an experimental option, `experimental.sri`, that checks script files by their hashes instead, so check its status before you rely on it.

## Sanitize what users write

A policy is a backstop. The front line is what React already does: it escapes text. The holes from the React course are the same here: `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, links whose `href` a user wrote and that start with `javascript:`, and Markdown turned into HTML. When you show Markdown a user wrote, like a review's body, turn it into HTML on the server and pass the result through a sanitizer such as DOMPurify or sanitize-html before it reaches the page.

examples.title: Security headers for every path
examples.prompt: `next.config.ts` with a Content Security Policy and four other security headers, set for every path.
examples.explanation: The policy is written as a list of directives joined with `; `, which is easier to read and change than one long string. `img-src` also allows `blob:` and `data:` addresses, which some image code uses, and `connect-src 'self'` lets the page's JavaScript fetch only from your own origin, which covers Server Actions and prefetches. `source: "/:path*"` matches every path, the root included. Because these headers live in the config, they apply to prerendered pages and files from `public/` as well, with no request-time work. Keep the other settings your config already had, like the Tailwind loader, next to these.

examples.title: The headers on a product page
examples.prompt: After a build, with the app running, ask for a product page's headers.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' blob: data:; font-src 'self'; connect-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()
x-request-id: 18efaf7a-8b35-4c55-8b24-d1b8b092f913
Vary: rsc, next-router-state-tree, next-router-prefetch, next-router-segment-prefetch, next-url, Accept-Encoding
link: </_next/static/media/07a39a8a4660cc7c-s.p.0r6juujl39pe6.woff2>; rel=preload; as="font"; crossorigin=""; type="font/woff2", </_next/static/media/605ce01b664af129-s.p.0wgildi0cnwt9.woff2>; rel=preload; as="font"; crossorigin=""; type="font/woff2"
x-nextjs-stale-time: 300
x-nextjs-prerender: 1
x-nextjs-postponed: 1
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidate
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Date: Sun, 22 Nov 2026 03:13:27 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: `-I` asks for the headers alone. The five security headers come first, exactly as the config wrote them, and `x-request-id` after them is the proxy's, from the lesson on Route Handlers and proxy. `X-Powered-By` is gone. `x-nextjs-prerender: 1` says the page's shell came from the prerendered copy, and `x-nextjs-postponed: 1` that its holes, like the stock count, were rendered for this request and streamed after it. That's why `Cache-Control` is `private, no-store`: the answer holds per-request parts. The config's headers went on it all the same, which is the point: static headers cost nothing per request and fit every kind of page. In the browser, DevTools' Network panel shows the same headers on the page's request, and the Console reports any content the policy blocks.

examples.title: A nonce for every response
examples.prompt: `proxy.ts` for a strict policy: a fresh nonce on each request, for pages that all render per request.
examples.explanation: `crypto.randomUUID()` makes a random ID, and base64 turns it into the nonce. `'strict-dynamic'` lets a script that carries the nonce load the other scripts it needs. The policy goes on the request, where Next.js reads the nonce while rendering and adds `nonce` to each script tag, and on the response, where the browser enforces it. `x-nonce` passes the nonce on so a Server Component can read it with `headers()` and give it to a third-party `Script`. The matcher skips API routes, built files, and prefetches, which don't need a policy. Run with the static policy's header removed and the root layout made dynamic, each script tag came back with a fresh `nonce` attribute, and the page hydrated.

steps.title: Keeping the framework patched
steps.body:
In a single-page app, a bug in React mostly breaks pages in the browser. In Next.js, React's server code and Next.js itself run on your server and read every request, including requests to Server Functions that anyone can send. A bug there is a hole in your server, however careful your own code is. Patching the framework is part of security, not housekeeping.

## React2Shell, December 2025

On December 3, 2025, React published CVE-2025-55182, soon nicknamed React2Shell, and rated it 10.0, the top of the scale. A crafted HTTP request to any Server Function endpoint could make the server run the attacker's code while React decoded the request's arguments, the serialized data from the Server Actions lesson. Apps with no Server Functions of their own were exposed too, as long as they used Server Components. It affected React's server packages, `react-server-dom-webpack`, `react-server-dom-parcel`, and `react-server-dom-turbopack`, in versions 19.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0, and it was fixed in 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1.

Next.js tracked it as CVE-2025-66478, for App Router apps on 15.x and 16.x. Each release line got a fixed version, from 15.0.5 to 15.5.7, and 16.0.7 for 16.0. Attacks started within days. Next.js told teams whose apps were online and unpatched on December 4 to rotate every secret the app used, since code running on your server can read its environment.

## The follow-ups

On December 11, 2025, React published three more. In CVE-2025-55184 and CVE-2025-67779, a crafted request sent the server into an endless loop, a **denial of service**: an attack that takes a site down without breaking in. The second was a case the first fix missed. In CVE-2025-55183, a request could make a Server Function send back its own source code, along with any secret written in it. On January 26, 2026, CVE-2026-23864 added another denial of service. The server packages' versions 19.0.4, 19.1.5, and 19.2.4 fix them all.

CVE-2025-55183 makes the case for the first part of this lesson. A key written in the code leaked with the source. A key read from `process.env` didn't.

Next.js ships its own copy of React's server code, so you patch it by updating `next` itself, and that's the package `npm audit` reports.

## npm audit, and bots that watch for you

`npm audit` compares your lockfile with the GitHub Advisory Database, the public list of known security bugs in packages, and reports the packages that are affected, as the React course showed. The example audits a lockfile pinned to Next.js 16.0.6, from just before React2Shell. Its suggested fix, `npm audit fix --force`, can jump to a much newer version, so read what it will install, then run your tests and a build before you ship.

Nobody runs `npm audit` every morning, so let a bot do it. **Dependabot**, built into GitHub, and **Renovate** open a **pull request**, a proposed change your team reviews before it joins the code, whenever a dependency has a new version or a security advisory, with its release notes attached. Your tests run on it, and you merge it. Watch the Next.js blog and the repository's security advisories too, since a 10.0 can't wait for the weekly update.

## Taint, a last line of defense

React has experimental **taint** APIs that make the server refuse to send a marked value or object to the browser: `experimental_taintUniqueValue` for a value like a key, and `experimental_taintObjectReference` for an object like a whole user record. They need `experimental: { taint: true }` in `next.config.ts`, which also switches the app to React's experimental releases. If any code then passes the marked value to a Client Component, React throws instead of sending it. Taint is a backstop for mistakes like the prop leak from part 2, never a replacement for DTOs: a copy of a tainted object isn't tainted, and neither is a value made from a tainted one.

examples.prompt: In a project whose lockfile pins `next` 16.0.6, `react` 19.2.0, and `react-dom` 19.2.0, ask npm for its audit report, the start and then the end. Mac and Linux.

npm audit | head -5
npm audit | tail -4

Severity: critical
Next.js is vulnerable to RCE in React flight protocol - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9qr9-h5gf-34mp

examples.explanation: `head -5` shows the start of the report and `tail -4` its end. The project's `package.json` pins `next` at 16.0.6. The report groups advisories by package: `next` from 9.3.4-canary.0 up to 16.4.4 is affected by something, and the worst is critical. The first advisory listed is React2Shell, under its GitHub ID, GHSA-9qr9-h5gf-34mp. RCE stands for remote code execution, running an attacker's code on your server, and the flight protocol is React's name for the RSC payload format. The full report lists 48 advisories for `next` alone, plus two packages it depends on, `postcss` and `sharp`, all fixed by one update of `next`. The same audit on the course's project, on 16.4.6, says found 0 vulnerabilities.

examples.title: Tainting the secret key
examples.prompt: `lib/env.ts` again, marking the rates API key so React refuses to send it to the browser.
examples.explanation: This is `lib/env.ts` with one more call, for an app with `experimental.taint` turned on. `experimental_taintUniqueValue` takes a message, an object whose lifetime the taint lasts for, and the value. Passing `process`, which lives as long as the server does, keeps the key tainted for good. If the prop leak from part 2 came back, the page would fail with this message instead of putting the key in the HTML, so the mistake shows up in development, not in a breach report. It's experimental, so check its status in the React and Next.js docs before you depend on it. With the secrets kept and every door checked, the next section gets the shop ready for visitors, starting with what search engines and link previews see before anyone clicks.

recap:
- Next.js loads .env files into process.env in a fixed order, and a variable set in the terminal beats every file.
- NEXT_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the browser's JavaScript at build time, so they're public and frozen until the next build.
- A prerendered page reads process.env during the build, so read per-deploy values after await connection().
- Keep secrets in server-only modules checked with zod, call paid APIs from the server with caching, and never pass a key as a prop.
- A cached verifySession() in a server-only data access layer reads the session once per render, and DAL functions return DTOs.
- Check access in every page, action, and Route Handler, since proxy and layouts are never the only check.
- Send security headers from next.config.ts, and know that a nonce CSP makes every route render per request.
- Framework bugs are server bugs: update next quickly, with npm audit and Dependabot or Renovate watching.
